#540. Feds arrest top official of healthcare company, alleging illegal drug importation

U.S. authorities are accusing the two top officials of a Canadian company of operating a long-running scheme to illegally import prescription drugs into the U.S., according to court records filed Tuesday.

John Thomas Howard, treasurer and a director of the company, CANARX, was arrested Sunday on smuggling and conspiracy charges, according to the records.

Bob Howard, his brother, who is president and a director of CANARX, is also wanted in the federal investigation, according to an affidavit from Dustin Dobbs, a special agent with the Food and Drug Administration's Office of Criminal Investigations. He has not yet been taken into custody.

Besides conspiracy and smuggling, the arrest warrant said John Thomas Howard was charged with introducing misbranded drugs into interstate commerce and illegal drug importation. No plea has been filed.

CANARX was featured in a CNBC investigation last year that revealed how the company and others known as alternative funding programs, or AFPs, are becoming more pervasive around the U.S. as drug costs skyrocket. The investigation found these companies have penetrated the country's healthcare system by offering high-cost specialty drugs at more affordable prices through private and public employers. In some cases, employers are requiring their staff to use an AFP.

AFPs often obtain the medications overseas and ship them directly to patients, a practice that federal authorities have said is illegal and poses safety risks. CNBC traced the trail of drugs from abroad to the U.S. via a supply chain that the pharmaceutical companies producing the medications have not authorized.

On its website, CANARX, founded in 2002 and based in Windsor, Ontario, Canada, described its business as the first international prescription provider for the U.S. and the safest such program in the industry. The company said it sources its medications from Canada, the United Kingdom, Australia and New Zealand.

But the affidavit said that the FDA's investigation found "there is probable cause to believe that (CANARX) illegally imported or caused the illegal importation of prescription drugs into the United States …."

The affidavit does not specify which medications the agency believes were illegally imported. The criminal complaint covers the period from Feb. 22, 2017, through April 15, 2026.

The company's general counsel, Joseph Morris, told CNBC in a statement: "The Howards deny all the charges against them, will defend vigorously, and expect to be vindicated in court."

The company has been under FDA scrutiny for several years. In 2023, the agency seized medication being shipped by CANARX that it says was potentially misbranded and counterfeit, according to an email sent to a patient that was obtained by CNBC.

And in 2019, the FDA sent a warning letter to the company, saying it was operating "in a manner that substitutes the FDA-approved drugs prescribed by the U.S. healthcare provider with unapproved drugs." Morris, in response to that warning, argued CANARX was not misleading patients, but agreed for the company to stop importing drugs that need to be administered by a doctor.

In an interview as part of the CNBC investigation, Morris said last year that the medicines shipped to U.S. patients come from highly regulated countries. He said CANARX was operating legally.

The central question for AFPs is the legality of importing prescription drugs into the U.S. for personal use. The FDA allows Americans to import medications for individual use in some cases if the drug is not available domestically. That is the basis on which the AFPs built their models for shipping medicines directly to patients.

But an FDA spokesperson told CNBC last year that "in most circumstances, a person cannot import prescription drugs from other countries into the U.S. ... as substitutes for FDA-approved drugs."

In a separate civil lawsuit that is pending, Gilead Sciences accused CANARX and other companies of illegally importing Biktarvy, its medication to treat HIV.

In a statement to CNBC on Wednesday, a Gilead spokesperson said the company "has taken strong legal action to protect patients and the integrity of the U.S. medicines supply chain. We welcome the government's efforts to hold accountable those whose conduct may put patients at risk."

CANARX has not responded to the Gilead lawsuit.

— CNBC's Paige Tortorelli and Melissa Lee contributed to this report

#527. Scout Motors has 212,000 vehicle reservations as $2 billion South Carolina plant nears completion

BLYTHEWOOD, S.C. — Electric vehicle startup Scout Motors has notched roughly 212,000 reservations for its upcoming EVs as the company nears completion of its new $2 billion plant here, CEO Scott Keogh told CNBC.

The reservations are for the Volkswagen-backed company's Terra pickup truck and Traveler SUV, which are expected to start full production next year before deliveries begin to customers in 2028.

Reservations do not necessarily translate to sales, as the U.S. automotive industry has learned during the past decade, especially with highly anticipated all-electric trucks such as the Ford F-150 Lightning, Tesla Cybertruck and others that garnered strong interest that didn't lead to meaningful numbers of purchases.

Keogh said he expects Scout could roughly double those reservations by the time customer production begins, but he said the more important thing is to convert early interest into actual sales as production nears.

"It's been a consistent drumbeat," Keogh said during an interview at Scout's plant site outside Columbia. "I think we could easily be up over 400,000 with reservations without doing too much effort. The big thing for us is how much of the initial production can we 100% presell."

Keogh said achieving an order book of 12 to 18 months "would be great" and is something he thinks the company can do before production. Scout on Thursday said plant construction is "in its final phase."

Scout's vehicles will be offered as all-electric versions as well as electric hybrid variants, known as extended-range electric vehicles, or EREVs, that include an internal combustion engine as a backup generator for the electric motors and batteries.

Scout, a former American vehicle brand from 1961 to 1980, was expected to exclusively offer EVs in a bid for the German automaker to expand its presence in the U.S. However, slower-than-expected adoption of EVs and higher costs led the company to decide to offer EREVs as well.

Keogh said extended-range and SUV models are dominating reservations thus far, with roughly 87% choosing EREV models and 75% being SUVs.

The CEO also said the company is drawing interest from its target markets, which include owners of off-road vehicles such as the Ford Bronco and Jeep Wrangler as well as full-size pickup trucks and U.S. EV leader Tesla.

Given the interest signaled by reservations, Keogh said the company is expected to launch with the EREVs first, followed by the EVs. He also said the company plans to launch with mid-level models first, a deviation from many companies that begin with their highest-priced models.

Both the Traveler and Terra are expected to start at under $60,000. The EREV models are expected to feature more than 500 miles of range, according to the company, compared with 300 miles of range for the all-electric models.

"The No.1 thing for me is I want to go get the best volume as soon as possible," Keogh said. "In my mind, it's how quick can you get to 100,000 units? It's at 100,000 units where you can start to punch through."

His comments come months after Rivian Automotive received criticism online for launching its R2 SUV with its highest-priced models first, despite that being a common practice across the automotive industry.

Keogh said Scout's South Carolina plant is about 85% complete, but supporting infrastructure and a $300 million supplier park continue to be installed.

Reservations for Scout's vehicles initially opened in October 2024, when it revealed the Traveler and Terra, which feature sleek, yet rugged, exteriors that pay some homage to the brand's historic models.

#524. Disney's 'Star Wars' is coming to Cosm domes ahead of 50th anniversary as part of multiyear film deal

On Thursday, the immersive entertainment technology company announced a new studio partnership with The Walt Disney Co. that will bring the original "Star Wars" to its domes early next year as part of a multiyear, multifilm collaboration.

The financial terms of the deal were not disclosed.

Cosm's massive concave screens will drop film fans into a galaxy far, far away starting in March, just ahead of the Academy Award-winning film's 50th anniversary in May.

"We are thrilled to add the Disney partnership," Alexis Scalice, head of Cosm Studios, told CNBC. "We do look for those opportunities of these like anniversary and commemorative moments. We look for those opportunities to celebrate with the fans, but also find this mutually beneficial partnership between both parties."

This will be Cosm's sixth theatrical collaboration with Hollywood, having already partnered with Warner Bros. to bring "The Matrix," "Willy Wonka & the Chocolate Factory," "Harry Potter and the Sorcerer's Stone" and "It" to its locations. The company is set to launch immersive screenings of Universal's "Shrek" in December.

Each Cosm dome has stadium-style seating, with booths and tables set on each level. The dome's width fills much of the viewers' periphery, giving the sensation that they are part of the onscreen environment.

In this case, "Star Wars" will be displayed in a large rectangle in the center of the dome while the background is transformed into the iconic planets of Tatooine and Yavin IV that are featured in the film as well as the infamous Death Star. Audiences will also see elements that will make it appear like they're traveling at lightspeed and getting trapped in an intergalactic trash compactor.

Cosm is working directly with studios Lucasfilm and Industrial Light and Magic as well as creative studio MakeMake to create the visuals and the sound mixing for the unique presentation of the film.

"We look for those moments where sound, music ... listening to Darth Vader's breath for the first time ... you feel those moments differently in an 87-foot diameter dome and 12k resolution with the sound system we have," Scalice said. "And it's one of the things that with experiential cinema and our technology that we were so excited and honestly privileged that we can take these defining moments for fans and work closely with our partners that doesn't really change the authenticity of it, it just enhances it in a different manner."

The premium experience will also be paired with a themed menu. Cosm has done this with other titles, such as "Harry Potter and the Sorcerer's Stone," serving guests throughout the screening with house-made shepherd's pie, pretzel wands with cheese dip and a box of Bertie Bott's Every Flavour Beans.

Cosm is trying to establish itself as a destination for fandom — both for sports and for film. It has a wide variety of live event offerings, which it telecasts using proprietary cameras mounted in arenas that broadcast back to the dome, as well as its expanding library of movies.

"What I love is that we really are kind of building these Cosm communities built on fandom," Scalice said. "It's the No. 1 foundation for our business."

And Star Wars is a powerful fandom. The franchise remains one of the top-ranking pieces of intellectual property across film, television and retail annually, and Disney is gearing up for a massive celebration of its semicentennial including merchandise launches, theatrical re-releases, its biannual Star Wars Celebration convention and collaborations with other brands.

Correction: This story has been updated to correct the spelling of Alexis Scalice's name.

#522. Everything to know about Black Friday 2026: Best early deals, sale dates, how to shop smart, and more

We're officially less than two weeks away from one of the biggest shopping events of the year: Black Friday.

Though most sales officially kick off this week, deals have been rolling out for the past few weeks. However, price trends are inching ever closer to record lows, harkening the true start to peak Black Friday season.

That doesn't necessarily mean you should start frantically adding deals to your cart right this instant, but it does mean that it's good to head into the mega-sale event with a plan. From knowing when sales from retailers like Amazon and Best Buy start to knowing which products will likely go on sale to preparing your own shopping list, we've got you covered on everything you need to know ahead of Black Friday and Cyber Monday.

This year, Black Friday falls on Nov. 27. While retailers often start featuring their best markdowns on Black Friday itself, there are plenty of early deals worth shopping in the lead-up. Most retailers' official sales do start before the actual day, so shopping strategically ahead of time can save you from missing out on a deal entirely (or dealing with the chaos the day after Thanksgiving).

Absolutely yes. The mega-retailer's sale kicks off Thursday, Nov. 19 — more info on the full date range of the sale is below. Expect deals on everything from the year's top tech to home essentials. Naturally, Amazon's devices also get markdowns across the board. So far, the retailer has teased the following:

Save up to 45% on Amazon's 2024 Kindle Colorsoft, 55-inch Ember Artline TV, and 55-inch Ember Mini LED-Series TV

Save up to 50% on select headphones and speakers from Beats, JBL, Marshall, and Sonos

Save up to 40% on select Ninja appliances, including the Creami, Foodi, and Slushi

Save up to 40% on select iRobot and Bissell floorcare

Save up to $500 on select Balsam Hill and Fraser Hill Farm artificial Christmas trees

Amazon: Amazon's Black Friday sale runs from Thursday, Nov. 19 to Nov. 30, offering 12 consecutive days of deals. Each day of the sale will feature "Today's Big Deals," where select products will be on sale for up to 60% off, except for on Black Friday and Cyber Monday proper. One batch of deals will go live at 3 a.m. ET, while another will go on sale at 11 a.m. ET.

Best Buy: Black Friday at Best Buy starts on Nov. 19, and runs through Saturday, Nov. 28. Its Cyber Monday sale runs from Nov. 29 to Nov. 30, with a Cyber Week sale that extends savings from Dec. 1 to Dec. 6. Total and Plus members of the My Best Buy program are also eligible to earn double points on their purchases from Nov. 19 to Dec. 6.

Walmart: Walmart has three major sale events throughout November: the early Black Friday sale from Nov. 12 to Nov. 15, the Black Friday sale from Nov. 23 to Nov. 29 (with deals online only from Nov. 23 to Nov. 26), and the online-only Cyber Monday sale from Nov. 30 to Dec. 2.

Target: Target hasn't released its full Black Friday lineup yet, but we do know its first Early Black Friday sale kicks off Nov. 5 to Nov. 7. From Nov. 1 to Dec. 24, Target's Deal of the Day offer kicks off, featuring new deals every day. Every weekend after Nov. 7, the retailer will also drop new limited-time holiday offers.

Considering prices went up this year on pretty much Apple devices except for AirPods, Black Friday will be the time to pick up new Apple devices. The short answer: Apple products will absolutely be on sale this Black Friday. The slightly longer answer: the best place to pick up Apple products during Black Friday sales will be at retailers like Amazon, Walmart, or Best Buy, which often duke it out to see who will drop a MacBook or pair of AirPods to the record-low price first (or, more impressively, keep it in stock the longest). Already in the lead-up, MacBooks are $250 off, and the AirPods Pro 3 are $70 off.

As for Apple itself holding Black Friday sales, the Apple Store features its own Black Friday sale every year: a free gift card for future use with the purchase of select devices. #520. Retailers are turning to entertainment to win shoppers’ attention

Legacy retailer Gap Inc. made an unconventional hire earlier this year: a chief entertainment officer.

It was a newly created role as the company tapped former Paramount executive Pam Kaufman to helm its entertainment, content and licensing platform. Gap has since rolled out major campaigns, partnering with bands like Just Your Type and building on the success of last year's ads with girl group Katseye.

"Beloved brands have value beyond the products they sell. Consumers identify with them, trust them and want to be part of their world," Kaufman told CNBC in a statement. "The key is authenticity: Every extension has to reflect what the brand stands for and give its fans a meaningful new way to experience it."

She said it's part of a broader goal to emphasize what Gap calls "fashiontainment," a strategy to blend retail and entertainment to better align with consumers. Gap is part of a growing cohort of retailers investing in entertainment and experiences both in-store and through exclusive online content to drive engagement.

"Brands are stories, and we are the storytellers," CEO Richard Dickson said at the Goldman Sachs Global Consumer and Retail conference in September. "I think you could see that come to life when you look at some of the work that we've done, putting our brands in the center of culture and cultural conversation."

In another blending of retail and media, Mattel made waves a few years ago for its "Barbie" movie, building on the intellectual property of a decades-old fan favorite and drawing in massive box office success. At the time, Dickson was president and chief operating officer of the company, witnessing firsthand the sectors' intersection before departing for Gap.

"I think the post-Covid consumer attitude around shopping certainly evolved a lot," said Bryan Eshelman, who leads the retail practice at consulting firm AlixPartners. "It has gone from shopping as a fulfillment task to shopping, in many instances, more as an entertainment form."

Between experiences in physical stores and media campaigns featuring exclusive content, Eshelman said, retailers are getting more creative about the ways they're driving engagement and marketing.

"Community, at the end of the day, is one of the key ways to drive loyalty, so I think retailers of all types are trying to tap into some sense of community, some sense of lifestyle, some sense of belonging that's beyond the product that they offer," he said.

Branded entertainment has been around for a long time. Procter & Gamble made headlines in the 1930s for helping to coin the term "soap opera," and companies have for decades created media campaigns to draw in customers.

But with the rise of social media, content creation and short-form offerings, experts said audiences are becoming hungrier than ever for something new and original.

The retail and entertainment intersection is happening at a time when intellectual property is becoming more valuable than ever, according to experts.

As consumers encounter more marketing than ever, the companies that will win the battle for attention are the ones that can "cut through all of the noise," said Alex Michael, senior managing director at investment firm LionTree.

"The hardest thing to find and to get is audience these days," Michael told CNBC. "IP, in that sense, is the most valuable thing out there, and only becoming more valuable because it's attached to audience."

At the same time, he said, the way IP is distributed is broadening to include video, audio, short-form, long-form and live event content. Consumers are also redefining their loyalty to brands, which means companies have to "play much earlier in the consumer journey" than they have in years past to secure their trust, he said.

The trend is also likely helped by executives who have worked in both retail and entertainment: Gap's Kaufman came from Paramount, for example, and Dickson and Skydance co-CEO Ynon Kreiz held top roles at Mattel.

"The gray areas have never been more pronounced as to what is classically defined as retail or media or entertainment or live events," Michael said. "People who have cross-sector expertise are increasingly more valuable because you can't be defined by a single vertical, especially as things change so quickly."

Still, there's room for newer players, especially with the studio landscape rapidly changing, said Sean Akaks, the CEO of SonderCo, an agency that partners brands with celebrities and entertainment properties.

"I think it's a really interesting time for nontraditional players to be making content because you're seeing this massive consolidation of these legacy entertainment companies," he said. "I think there are just more open lanes for independent creators and also brands and anyone outside the traditional studio system to create content."

That's where retailers might tap creators, Akaks said, because they can use their platforms to reach consumers directly.

"I do think there's a world where we're going to see creators and brands sort of co-creating IP that maybe they're owning together," he said.

Once those companies get consumers into the store, they're also leaning into experiential retail, making shopping a more immersive experience than it otherwise would be, like Dick's Sporting Goods offering interactive activities and simulators in its stores.

According to data from AlixPartners, companies investing in experiential retail such as Coach and Ralph Lauren saw close to 10% year-over-year increases in consumers' average basket size.

"The idea that retailers would potentially invest in some distributed electronic content to help drive traffic, and then when you get there, it's experiential — it really goes into the kinds of flywheels that entertainment companies are also trying to build and grow," said Jeff Goldstein, co-lead of the media and entertainment practice at AlixPartners.

Yet, the entertainment that retail brands are developing is only one piece in a larger puzzle to retain customers and attract new ones. Translating that into tangible sales growth isn't necessarily a given.

"The basics of having great product in stock at a transparent price that feels like value is not swept away by animatronics," AlixPartners' Eshelman said. "The fundamentals are still there, and if you're going to have a good retail proposition, you need to have that balance. You can't mask bad product at a bad price with no inventory with glitz and glamour."

#517. While Rome burns, United is worried about you using AI to book a flight

The incessant trouble in the airline industry reached a peak on Friday when the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) issued a rare nationwide ground stop, halting U.S. air traffic for more than four hours due to a critical telecommunications and network outage.

It was a nightmare trying to get the flights back to normal over the weekend, and then on Monday, United Airlines reported a system outage that they eventually rectified.

Chaos is the operative word for airlines these days, with near misses in the air, and increasing delays and cancellations. Amid all these industry pressures, United has another concern: The airline isn’t happy with passengers who rely on their AI chatbots to make reservations.

First, let’s step back to just a few weeks ago, when United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby went on a podcast to brag about his latest personal breakthrough. After just three hour-long sessions with an AI tutor, the airline executive taught himself to "vibe-code" a custom sports-betting app, a tool designed to compare odds across platforms and automatically place bets on his behalf.

He called it an "AI epiphany." Apparently, that epiphany only applies when the guy running the airline is using AI to hunt for better odds.

Which raises a rather curious question in my mind. If the CEO of a major airline builds his own automated betting tool, does that come with any guardrails? Pro athletes get lifetime bans for wagering on their own games, so one has to hope Kirby’s vibe-coded bot isn't quietly placing action on prediction markets for "percentage of United flights delayed out of Newark."

Now, I’m not accusing the guy of shaving points on departure times (or an unexpected system outage), though it might explain a recent long delay I had flying out of Newark. All stated in fun, but I digress.

Recently, United updated its Contract of Carriage to explicitly ban third-party AI agents, like OpenAI’s Dots and Meta’s Muse, from booking, changing, or managing flights on behalf of passengers.

Even if you're sitting right there supervising the transaction, United says that using a personal AI assistant to manage your trip is a no-go. Specifically, it means that United now classifies your reservation as a prohibited ticketing practice, giving the airline the legal right to cancel your trip without notice, confiscate your frequent flyer miles, and refuse to let you board.

Wow, sounds like United really, really hates it when you use AI. Which is odd, because the travel and hospitality industry — read United — has spent the last few years aggressively handing off reservation desks, customer support, and administrative jobs to AI.

So, let me get this straight. Is United suddenly preaching the irreplaceable value of the human touch? The airline cited data security, the risk of "unintended purchases," and federal rules requiring passengers to personally attest during check-in that their bags don't contain explosives as reasons for opposing chatbot purchasing.

OK, I get that. It makes sense. Well, sort of. Because, to me, what's actually happening here is that United isn't anti-AI. What I think United really means is, "Don't use AI, unless it's ours."

If you've tried to rebook a canceled flight, dispute a baggage fee, or simply get a straight answer from an airline lately, you know how cumbersome the process is. You aren't talking to a human being. You're stuck in an endless loop with a clunky corporate chatbot or navigating an automated phone tree. Now, to be honest, have you ever done any of that successfully on your own without eventually having to speak with someone? The best tech deal this week The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile Products available for purchase through affiliate links. If you buy something through links on our site, Mashable may earn an affiliate commission.

The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile

I didn't think so. I think the whole thing is actually designed to make you give up before reaching a real person.

For years, major airlines, again, read United, have aggressively automated away human reservation desks, contact centers, and management roles in the name of efficiency. They're also using AI behind the scenes to track your habits and tweak ticket prices on the fly — pun intended. What they're trying to do is make sure you pay the absolute maximum you're willing to fork over.

The rise of agentic AI, bots that don't just summarize emails but actively browse the web, click buttons, and execute tasks for you, threatens to flip that behind-the-scenes tracking on its head. For the first time, regular people have access to automated tools that can finally fight bots with bots.

An AI agent working for you, and not the airline, doesn't get tired of refreshing flight pages to catch a $40 fare drop. It doesn't forget to apply your travel credits, and it won't cave to endless pop-ups begging you to pay extra for a carry-on bag or a seat assignment.

Worse yet, from an airline's perspective, a personal AI assistant strips away the airline's direct marketing funnel. As Kirby candidly admitted at an event in Chicago on Tuesday, "To be honest, I don't want to create another middleman."

For decades, airlines systematically cut commissions and squeezed out traditional human travel agents. I guess you could say they were the original "middlemen." Airlines hated paying someone else to advocate for the passenger.

Now, agentic AI is essentially giving every traveler a free digital travel agent. Why would airlines eliminate human travel agents just to let ChatGPT or Meta take their place?

And that brings us to the ultimate corporate double standard of the AI era.

When companies use AI to replace human booking agents, slash support staff, and jack up ticket prices, it's framed as "innovation." Workers lose their jobs, and customers are told to just deal with the bots left behind.

Yet the moment travelers deploy their own AI agents to hunt for cheaper fares, corporations slam the door shut, suddenly citing safety, compliance, and the sacred necessity of human involvement.

You can expect banks, retailers, and hotels to copy United's ban and continue replacing human workers with bots, all the while forcing shoppers to just deal with them.

Until companies give back the human customer service they took away, banning our bots isn't really about protecting travelers. After all, as any guy with a custom sports-betting app knows, the real goal is making sure the house always wins.

This article represents the opinions of its writer.

John Casey is a columnist at Raw Story, the Advocate, Daily Beast, and Outsports. He's also the author of Love: The Heroic Stories of Marriage Equality.

#514. Eric Trump-backed robot soldier startup can't pay staff after founder borrowed $4.6 million from company to buy home

Foundation Future Industries, a maker of military humanoid robots advised and backed by Eric Trump, failed to pay employees last month as its cash reserves dwindled, according to people with direct knowledge of the matter.

Workers have yet to receive paychecks after San Francisco-based Foundation missed payroll on Oct. 30, said the people, who asked for anonymity to speak candidly about a private company.

The situation has particularly angered some inside the startup because its co-founder and CEO, Sankaet Pathak, borrowed $4.6 million from the company last year to buy a luxury home, money that could have been used to pay workers, the people said.

Public records show that an LLC that names Pathak as sole principal purchased a $4.6 million Sausalito, California, property with "sweeping, cinematic views" of the San Francisco Bay in October 2025.

A spokesman for Pathak acknowledged receiving a detailed list of the major points from this story on Thursday, but didn't respond to requests for comment. Pathak's previous startup, a fintech firm named Synapse, collapsed in 2024, leaving thousands of Americans locked out of their savings accounts.

Foundation's cash crunch comes at a precarious moment for the company, which Pathak has said is close to unveiling a next-generation, weapons-ready robot that will help the U.S. compete against Chinese rivals. At the same time, Pathak is seeking to raise hundreds of millions of dollars in funding at a $3 billion valuation.

The company has garnered headlines this year for Pathak's claims that his robots could soon take on battlefield tasks in Ukraine or patrol the U.S. border with Mexico. Broadcast interviews and articles about Foundation also include claims that the company has won $24 million in Pentagon contracts.

"What we're about to unveil in the next couple of months [is] going to be the strongest humanoid robot that exists anywhere in the world, including China," Pathak said in an April television interview.

That April interview introduced Eric Trump, the son of the U.S. president, as a Foundation investor and chief strategy advisor. It is unclear how large his stake is.

Eric Trump and his brother Donald Trump Jr. have invested in an array of defense firms, including makers of military drones and autonomous weapons. A July Washington Post investigation found that startups backed by investment vehicles linked to the brothers had secured at least $3.2 billion in government business.

"We have to win robotics in the United States of America," Eric Trump said in April. "When you go up and interact with these robots ... they fist bump you, they high-five you, they follow your commands."

Eric Trump's involvement in Foundation drew the swift ire of Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., who asked whether Foundation won U.S. defense contracts because of nepotism.

"Eric Trump went on FOX to brag about winning ANOTHER multimillion-dollar contract from the Trump administration," Warren said in an April 23 social media post. "This looks like corruption in plain sight."

Eric Trump didn't respond to requests for comment. His spokesperson recently told the Financial Times that Eric Trump had "no involvement in Foundation's management, operations, strategic decisions or commercial activities, including the solicitation, negotiation, procurement or execution of any government contracts."

While the Eric Trump announcement created speculation within Foundation that a Democratic-led Congress may look to investigate the company, Foundation itself didn't actually win the $24 million in contracts, despite that assertion being widely reported across news outlets.

Instead, it acquired Florida-based Boardwalk Robotics in late 2024, and government research contracts won by that firm account for the claim, said a person with knowledge of the matter. Foundation used Boardwalk's robot Alex as the basis for its first robot, the Phantom MK-1, this person said.

Foundation's deal for Boardwalk included performance milestones for the robot that haven't been reached, said a separate person with direct knowledge of the deal.

In 2024, CNBC reported that letters Pathak sent to prospective investors cited an imminent investment and $300 million purchase order from General Motors, claims the automaker rejected.

Foundation co-founder Mike LeBlanc said at the time he was "embarrassed" about the marketing materials.

Insiders fret that Foundation could soon fold if Pathak doesn't secure fresh funding. Pathak has been seeking to raise hundreds of millions of dollars at a $3 billion valuation since at least January.

Pathak is Foundation's sole board member, a structure that has raised concerns among prospective investors about corporate governance, said the people familiar with the matter. He also owns most of the firm's shares.

That setup allowed Pathak to borrow $4.6 million last year, which he called a short-term loan at the time, the people said. Existing investors are aware of the loan through the company's financial disclosures, the people said.

"This is what happens in a company with no governance," said one of the people. "Are you just going to let it ride into the ground, and you ride off into the sunset?"

Foundation also ran out of cash for payroll in August, though employees only had to wait about two days to get paid after the company secured a bridge loan from an existing investor, the people said.

Pathak told employees this week in a memo that he was working on sourcing money to pay back wages.

The company was founded in April 2024 by Pathak, Tribe Capital CEO Arjun Sethi and LeBlanc, co-founder of Cobalt Robotics, a maker of autonomous security guards, according to a fundraising pitch at the time.

Foundation went on to hire dozens of robotics engineers and artificial intelligence experts, managing to lure some from Tesla and Amazon-owned autonomous vehicle company Zoox.

Before Foundation, Pathak was known as the founder of Synapse, a kind of middleman that enabled fintech firms like Mercury, Dave and YieldStreet to offer savings accounts and credit cards with the help of small community banks.

Synapse was a behind-the-scenes player until its collapse left more than 100,000 Americans with a combined $265 million in deposits locked out of their Federal Deposit Insurance Corp.-backed accounts.

While some customers received partial payments during Synapse's bankruptcy proceedings, thousands remain without access to their money after more than two years. A bankruptcy trustee, the former FDIC Chair Jelena McWilliams, said as much as $96 million in customer funds went missing.

The bankruptcy proceedings concluded last year without uncovering where the funds went; Pathak blamed a banking partner named Evolve, and Evolve blamed Synapse for the mess. U.S. regulators didn't intervene until the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau sued Synapse last year, opening up a $55 million fund for customer relief.

Pathak withdrew $320,000 in loans from Synapse as it spiraled toward bankruptcy in 2024 amid disputes over unmatched ledgers, according to the consultant and independent journalist Jason Mikula.

Federal prosecutors convened a grand jury to investigate possible criminal misconduct at Synapse, The Wall Street Journal reported last year. The Journal report didn't mention Pathak specifically.

The controversy didn't dissuade Eric Trump from investing in Foundation and Pathak, who he called a friend in the April broadcast interview.

"I walked into his factory, and I couldn't believe what I saw," Eric Trump said. "I'm telling you, he's doing a phenomenal job."

#513. The best MacBook to buy in 2026: Heres who should upgrade to the new OLED MacBook Pro

MacBooks have been ridiculously easy to recommend since we first started reviewing them in the mid-2010s, but especially since Apple rolled out its first M-series chips in 2020. That custom silicon affords them much faster, quieter performance than most competing Windows PCs. When you factor in their elite build quality, beautiful displays, solid battery life, and polished operating system, it's little wonder that MacBooks are some of the most well-loved laptops.

This fall, Apple launched two new MacBook Pros — including its first with an OLED touchscreen display. After hands-on testing the entire current lineup, these are the best MacBooks we recommend for different kinds of users.

These are the tech, tools, and products — from laptops to e-readers, from earbuds to robovacs, and more — that Mashable ranks best in class.

The 15-inch M5 MacBook Air is the best MacBook for most people. It's a sleek, future-proofed ultraportable with the right amount of premium features and more than enough muscle for everyday multitasking, including occasional content creation. It's the ideal daily driver.

You might also consider the 13-inch M5 MacBook Air, which is slightly cheaper and more portable. We think it's the best MacBook for college students.

The MacBook Neo is our top pick for budget shoppers, casual users, and younger students. It's not nearly as fast or as fancy as a MacBook Air, but it's a good performer for its price point, and it's just as well-made as any other MacBook. If your typical workload involves bopping between some Chrome tabs and an app or two, look no further.

The 14-inch M6 MacBook Pro is our upgrade pick for power users with consistently heavy workloads and a moderate amount of wiggle room in their budgets. (Realistically, it's the best MacBook Pro for most people.) The best tech deal this week The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile

The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile

The only users who should splurge on the new touch-enabled MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display are professional creatives who primarily use their computer for intensive visual and design work. We recommend going with the 16-inch model for the maximum screen space — its tandem OLED display is just that good.

Apple raised the prices of all of its MacBooks this summer — thanks, RAMageddon — and the new MacBook Pros are quite expensive. Even the M6 base model costs $2,000. If you're mulling an upgrade, be sure to keep a close eye on Black Friday sales: Most retailers save their most competitive MacBook deals for the year-end holiday season.

Here are the Black Friday MacBook deals we expect to see in the coming weeks, based on our coverage of last year's sales and, in the case of the MacBook Neo, our wishful thinking. (The Neo wasn't around for Black Friday 2025, but it's due for a discount of at least $50 at this point in its lifecycle.)

For a deeper dive into all of our best MacBook picks, read on.

Apple's latest MacBook Air packs the snappy performance of the M5 chip inside a predictably polished and portable design. It's a great daily driver that can do basically anything the average person needs a laptop for, making it the best MacBook for everyday use. Yes, it's several hundred dollars pricier than a MacBook Neo, but it's a much better, more future-proofed computer in every way.

I think most folks will make good use of the larger screen on the 15-inch M5 MacBook Air, which starts at $1,499. It's configurable with up to 32GB of RAM and up to 4TB of storage.

Read Mashable's full review of the 15-inch Apple MacBook Air (M5).

The M5 MacBook Air successfully beats the awkward middle child allegations. It easily handles the workloads of everyday multitaskers, and it has some premium features that won't feel outdated in a few years (without going too overboard on nice-to-haves).

Performance-wise, this is one of the fastest laptops on the market no matter how you stack it. It zips through simpler single-core tasks like web browsing, and isn't intimidated by heavy multi-core workloads like video editing. Just be mindful that too much of the latter can make it warm and cause thermal throttling — it's fanless, after all. The MacBook Pros have fans, so they're better at handling the stress of creative apps and games over longer periods of time.

The M5 MacBook Air lasted 17 hours and 40 minutes in our battery life benchmark, which is a video rundown test. That's a small downgrade from the last generation, but you won't be screwed if you forget your charger at home.

Aesthetically, this is largely the same laptop as the M4 MacBook Air, which isn't a terrible thing, since that laptop slapped. (It just makes for a boring gen-over-gen update.) It has a crisp 12MP Center Stage webcam, a vivid Liquid Retina display, amazing speakers, a luxe haptic trackpad, a snappy backlit Magic Keyboard with Touch ID, and a sleek all-aluminum design. Like all MacBooks, its build quality is class-leading. You can take your pick from four neutral finishes: sky blue, silver, starlight, and midnight.

For its ultraportable design and slightly lower price tag, I deem the 13-inch M5 MacBook Air the best MacBook for college students — particularly liberal arts, humanities, nursing, and social science majors. (Your coursework probably doesn't require Windows.) The budget MacBook Neo can serve you well in the short term if you just need a basic laptop for writing essays and sending emails. But this compact Air is a smarter investment that will last you past graduation.

As a college student, you'll save $100 on the 13-inch MacBook Air with Apple's education discount. It starts at $1,199 with 16GB of RAM and 512GB of storage, which you can bump up to 32GB and 4TB, respectively.

Read PCMag's full review of the 13-inch Apple MacBook Air (M5). PCMag and Mashable are both owned by Ziff Davis.

The 13-inch M5 MacBook Air is just as fast and pretty as the 15-inch model, but easier to carry across campus (and a little nicer on your wallet).

There are only a couple minor differences between the two sizes. The 13-incher has two fewer speakers, and its base model has a lesser GPU with two fewer cores (eight versus 10), making it a hair worse for stuff like light video editing and gaming. Otherwise, their performance and specs are identical. It comes in the same four colorways, too.

The MacBook Neo is the best choice for budget buyers and casual users, including K-12 students. It's not as well-rounded as a MacBook Air, but it's an amazing starter laptop with the same great build quality (and livelier color options). It also makes a good secondary laptop for entertainment and online shopping if your daily driver lives at the office.

The MacBook Neo comes in two configurations. There's a $699 base model with 256GB of storage, and a $799 version that doubles your disk space and adds Touch ID.

Read Mashable's full review of the Apple MacBook Neo.

The Neo doesn't have a ton of pizzazz or multitasking brawn, but it's great for what it is: a very cheap MacBook. It outclasses most similarly priced Windows laptops and Chromebooks.

Inside the Neo, you'll find an A18 Pro chip with a six-core CPU and a five-core GPU, which is a lesser version of the processor inside 2024's iPhone 16 Pro. A laptop running on a smartphone chip? How does that work? Very well, actually, per our benchmarking. (Modern smartphones have been holding their own against PCs for some time now.) In basic single-core tasks, the Neo scores on par with an M4 MacBook Air. In other words, it feels just as snappy as a much more expensive MacBook when you're browsing the web, sending emails, and streaming videos.

In heavy multi-core tasks like video editing, the Neo scores about as well as an M1 MacBook Air from 2020 — not too shabby. Mashable tech editor Timothy Beck Werth had no trouble using it for a simple Final Cut Pro edit. But keep in mind that its 8GB of fixed RAM is really going to limit your ability to juggle a bunch of apps or files. The archetypal Neo user will only have a couple of browser tabs open at any given time, maybe with Spotify running in the background. Anything too demanding will make it pokey.

The Neo lasts for around 15 hours per charge. It dies much sooner than an Air or Pro, but it'll definitely get you through a full workday with plenty of juice to spare.

The 13-inch Neo weighs the same as a 13-inch MacBook Air (which technically measures 13.6 inches across), but it's slightly thicker. It's also fanless, just like the Air. It has a pretty Liquid Retina display and excellent speakers with Dolby Atmos and Spatial Audio support. Its 1080p webcam is located in its upper bezel, so unlike a MacBook Air or base Pro, it doesn't have an uggo notch jutting down into its screen. Apple ditched features like keyboard backlighting, True Tone display technology, a haptic touchpad, and fast Thunderbolt ports in making the Neo affordable, but it didn't skimp on build quality. It has an all-aluminum design that makes it just as sturdy and polished as any other MacBook. (Most cheap laptops have plastic components.) It also comes in some fun colors like blush, citrus, and indigo.

The M6 MacBook Pro is our top pick for power users who are willing to pay a little extra for a smoother, brighter display, more ports, better speakers, and more sustained computing power. It's overkill for the average person, but it's worth the investment for most content creators, developers, AI enthusiasts, and other professionals who run demanding creative apps (plus the occasional game) on a regular basis.

The M6 MacBook Pro is available in one 14-inch size starting at $1,999 with 16GB of RAM and 1TB of storage. It maxes out with 32GB of RAM and 4TB of disk space. You can upgrade its display with a nano-texture (matte) finish for $150 extra.

Read Mashable's full review of the 14-inch Apple MacBook Pro (M6).

Some users will look at the M5 MacBook Air and find its specs a little lacking — more "adequate" than "amazing." For you, there's the M6 MacBook Pro.

The MacBook Air's M5 chip is no slouch by any means, but this guy's fresher M6 chip is even more powerful, especially in demanding multi-core workloads. And its fans make it better at handling them over a long period of time; thermal throttling is much more likely with an Air.

It's worth mentioning that Mashable's Timothy Beck Werth was able to play Cyberpunk 2077 on the M6 MacBook Pro at 30fps. I wouldn't buy it solely for this reason: Windows laptops are compatible with way more games than MacBooks, and PCs with discrete GPUs, especially, are much better-equipped to run graphically taxing titles. But just know that AAA gaming is possible here if you want to run the occasional mission after work.

Design-wise, the M6 MacBook Pro is slightly less portable than the Air, but not by much. It's less than 0.2 inches thicker than both sizes and 0.1 pounds heavier than the 15-inch model. This affords it enough room for extra fixings like an HDMI port, an SDXC card slot, and a bonus Thunderbolt port, as well as an awesome hi-fi sound system with force-cancelling woofers. I've tested dozens of laptops over the course of my career, and none of them sound better than a MacBook Pro.

The M5 MacBook Pro looks as spectacular as it sounds, as per tradition. (Apple hasn't made any drastic design changes to it since 2021.) Compared to the M5 MacBook Air's standard Liquid Retina screen, its mini-LED "Liquid Retina XDR" display is crisper, brighter, and smoother when displaying visuals in motion. Take your pick from two finishes: space black or silver. Be mindful that the former is a fingerprint magnet.

We haven't run our battery life test on the M6 MacBook Pro yet, but we have high expectations. Last year's M5 model held out for 21 hours and 17 minutes to become the longest-lasting MacBook we've ever tried.

Apple's all-new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display is geared toward deep-pocketed creative professionals whose work requires a ton of horsepower and a reference-quality display. (And, to a lesser extent, people who've missed MacBooks' glowing Apple logo, which hasn't been a thing since 2015.)

This beastly machine comes in a 14-inch size (starting at $2,899) and a 16-inch size (starting at $3,399) with an M5 Pro or M5 Max chip, 24GB to 128GB of RAM, and 1TB to 16TB of SSD storage. Both can be upgraded with a nano-texture display finish. We prefer the bigger model for the extra screen space.

Read Mashable's full review of the 16-inch Apple MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display (M5 Pro).

Its name is a mouthful, and its screen is an eyeful. Apple's all-new MacBook Pro has an elite tandem OLED display that wowed Mashable Tech Editor Timothy Beck Werth. "Apple hasn't just made an OLED laptop; it's made a genuine reference-quality display, designed to meet industry standards for video editors, photographers, animators, 3D artists, and color graders," he wrote. ("Reference-quality" refers to the fact that its colors are extremely lifelike and accurate.) It's an absolutely luscious display — not to mention super bright. It can hit up to 2,000 nits of peak HDR brightness, which makes it one of the brightest laptop displays ever made.

The new MacBook Pro's OLED display has touch capabilities, too, which is mainly interesting because it brings support for the Dynamic Island instead of a webcam notch. (And Apple execs' history of hating on touchscreen laptops, of course.) You can't use it as a tablet, nor does it support styluses. "If I were a betting man, I would wager that the touchscreen won't stick around forever," Werth said.

The model we tested ran on the M5 Pro, and our benchmarking showed that it's a macho, macho chip. In multi-core tasks, it whizzes past every laptop processor we've ever tried — in any MacBook or Windows PC. Compared to the M6 chip in the new base MacBook Pro, it offers a jaw-dropping 57 percent performance boost when running intensive software.

What's even more impressive is the fact that the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display doesn't heat up easily, despite being thinner and lighter than the standard MacBook Pros. The 16-inch model weighs in at four pounds — a whopping 0.7 pounds less than its non-OLED counterpart, which makes a real difference when you're working on the go.

The other main design differences between this model and the standard MacBook Pro are its glowing Apple logo and upgraded sound system, which "[provides] deeper bass and better clarity," Werth said. Their keyboards, trackpads, color options, webcams, mics, and port setups are the same.

Our battery life test results for the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display aren't finalized yet, but Apple rated it at up to 24 hours of video streaming (same as the regular Pro).

In November 2026, I added two new picks based on our latest round of testing. The M6 MacBook Pro is now our upgrade pick, and the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display is our new top pick for professional creatives. (Look for their battery life test results in the next update.) I also added information about Black Friday MacBook deals.

In August 2026, I updated this guide to reflect Apple's newly increased MacBook prices and named the 13-inch M5 MacBook Air our top pick for college students.

In May 2026, I added the results of our battery life testing for the M5 MacBook Air. It was able to loop a video for 17 hours and 40 minutes before dying.

MacBooks tend to go on sale at their deepest discounts during Amazon's summer Prime Day sale and around Black Friday. They also see steep price cuts as soon as they're no longer current-generation models, meaning right after Apple announces their successors (which usually happens every year in March and October.)

Apple hosts a Black Friday sale every year, but it just entails free gift card promotions. For proper price cuts, shop around at third-party retailers like Amazon and Best Buy.

First, a little info about how Apple classifies its older products. Devices that it stopped selling more than five years ago but less than seven are considered "vintage," whereas devices it stopped selling more than seven years ago are "obsolete."

Vintage MacBooks are still eligible for hardware support from Apple, depending on parts availability, but it won't fix obsolete MacBooks. And you can't get parts for them from third-party service providers like Best Buy and Micro Center.

If your obsolete MacBook is still chugging along like normal, is in good condition, and doesn't seem sluggish or scant on storage, by all means, keep using it. However, if any component breaks, deteriorates, or no longer meets your needs, it's time to send it off to the great MacBook farm in the sky. Consider recycling or donating it so it doesn't sit in a landfill.

While MacBooks don't get software updates forever, it's not a dealbreaker if yours can't run the latest version of macOS. You might be able to repurpose it as a streaming device or turn it into a Chromebook. That said, a MacBook you use as your primary laptop for school or work needs to be compatible with the current macOS in order to stay secure and continue running Apple apps.

FYI: The latest version of Apple's Mac operating system, macOS 27 (aka macOS Golden Gate), only works with M-series MacBooks from 2020 or later. That means if your daily driver is an older model with an Intel chip, it's high time to upgrade. It will still get security updates for the next two-ish years but won't support any new features going forward.

Some of the best Windows laptops and Chromebooks we've tested can rival MacBooks on performance and/or build quality. My favorite MacBook alternatives include the Asus Zenbook A14, the Dell XPS 13, and the Dell XPS 14.

If you want to stay within the Apple ecosystem, iPads also make good MacBook alternatives thanks to iPadOS's "windowing" system.

Mashable has been writing about laptops for over a decade, and I've personally been covering them since 2023. I also helped develop the rigorous hands-on testing process we currently use to review them. This methodology revolves around four criteria:

The laptops we review get put to work as our primary computers. This includes trying any unique software or use cases they support. We also subject all of our loaners to a multi-app/tab stress test and Primate Labs' Geekbench, which measures CPU performance in common tasks. Gaming laptops get put through additional graphical benchmarking.

To gauge a laptop's stamina, we conduct a battery rundown test that involves playing a looped 1080p version of "Tears of Steel," a short open-source Blender movie, at 50 percent brightness and 50 percent volume. Ideally, we hope to get at least 19 hours of battery life from MacBooks.

As we're using a laptop, we zero in on certain components to evaluate its build quality. These include the display, keyboard, touchpad, webcam, speakers, and ports. We also assess its overall aesthetic and portability.

We determine the ultimate value of a laptop by comparing its performance, design/build quality, and battery life to other laptops with similar pricing, specs, release dates, and use cases. We consider any accessories it comes with, any upgrades from its predecessor(s), and its future-proofing.

Haley Henschel is a Chicago-based Senior Shopping Reporter at Mashable who reviews and finds deals on popular tech, from laptops to gaming consoles and VPNs. She has years of experience covering shopping holidays and can tell you what’s actually worth buying on Black Friday and Amazon Prime Day. Her work has also explored the driving forces behind digital trends within the shopping sphere, from dupes to 12-foot skeletons.

#509. Rivian, Lucid, Scout CEOs aren’t counting on Democrats to restore EV federal support after midterm wins

Leaders of several U.S. electric vehicle manufacturers said they're not counting on increased federal support for their businesses once Democrats gain control of Congress in January, but they said they'll gladly take it if it does happen.

That was the overall sentiment from CEOs of Rivian Automotive, Lucid Group and EV startup Scout Motors during interviews with CNBC after Democrats' historic midterm election wins.

"We've honestly constructed Scout from day one to be in an environment where we're not going to count on, let's say, legislation or count on things that may or may not be there," Scout CEO Scott Keogh, an automotive veteran, told CNBC on Wednesday.

EV makers have had to contend with flip-flopping support from Washington over the years. The Trump administration has ended or rolled back support for climate change initiatives and EVs that were supported by the Biden administration, including an up to $7,500 customer incentive for purchasing an EV.

Legacy automakers such as General Motors and EV startups alike had counted on such credits to help them boost their sales and assist in electric vehicle profitability. But now they don't have that same level of federal assistance.

Rivian CEO RJ Scaringe said it's his hope that the Democratic-controlled Congress and Republican President Donald Trump can find middle ground to make progress for the EV industry, but Rivian's not counting on that.

"We try not to plan for those sort of things. The reality is it's probably going to have less of an impact than we think," Scaringe said Nov. 6 following the election results. "I think we're going to actually have a lot of challenges getting things done."

Fellow EV manufacturer Lucid, which is backed by Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund, is taking a similar approach.

"You know, they say, 'Plan for the worst and … hope for the best.' That's all we can say," Lucid CEO Silvio Napoli told CNBC on Monday. "Anything positive, we'll take it."

The lack of expected support comes as Democrats seem to be more focused on hot topics such as healthcare and data centers rather than climate change and support for alternative energy technologies such as EVs.

CNBC previously reported that House Democrats plan to bring to the floor bills reinstating the enhanced health insurance subsidies that expired under the GOP-held Congress and reversing the Medicaid cuts Trump signed into law last year. They also plan to focus on oversight of the Trump administration and affordability.

Rachel McCleery, executive director of the nonprofit policy advisory Coalition for Reimagined Mobility at SAFE, said she believes affordability concerns also could include the cost of vehicles, including EVs.

"I fully expect there will be legislative debates over what to do moving forward, including on EV and EV supply chain incentives," McCleery, a former U.S. Department of Treasury senior advisor and Ford Motor policy director, said. "Bringing down the cost of vehicles for U.S. consumers is top of mind for Democratic policymakers, and electric vehicles are a critical aspect of this agenda because of the multiple challenges greater EV adoption solves for."

Scout's Keogh said if legislators decide to offer any type of support, he would prefer it to be for EV production, which could then have a trickle-down effect on vehicle pricing and help companies amid inflated costs.

"I always prefer it on the production side," Keogh said. "Anything that can drive down production cost is going to, of course, get passed along to the customer."

Affordability has been a concern for EV adoption as the vehicles typically cost more than traditional models with internal combustion engines.

Sales of EVs spiked last year ahead of the Trump administration ending the up to $7,500 incentive after September 2025, but have since come down from that high.

Cox Automotive reports the average price for a new electric vehicle as of September was more than $54,800, according to the most recent available data. That compared to the average overall industry at just over $51,100 last month.

"Ultimately, incentives can help accelerate adoption, but the industry can't build its long-term strategy around them," Stephanie Valdez Streaty, Cox director of industry insight, said Friday. "The goal has to be making EVs affordable and compelling enough that they make sense for more consumers with or without an incentive."
