#347. ‘The Predators Are Real’: Senate Hearing Slams Roblox Over Child Sex Abuse

People who say they were groomed on Roblox testified in front of a Congressional subcommittee Tuesday about safety risks associated with the popular gaming platform frequented by kids and teenagers.

“Roblox is one of the most popular gaming platforms in the world,” Republican senator Josh Hawley said in his opening remarks. “If your children are on Roblox they are being exposed in all likelihood to sexual predators … to sexually exploitative content, left, right, and center.”

The hearing was intended to address the bipartisan legislation introduced by Hawley and Democratic senator Dick Durbin, coauthors of the No Forced Arbitration for Child Sexual Exploitation and Cyber Injuries Act, which would allow families of victims to sue Roblox directly instead of being forced to settle their claims privately in arbitration, as the platform’s terms of service currently dictate.

The process of forced arbitration “strips consumers and workers of their rights,” testified Myriam Gilles, a law professor at Northwestern University who is an expert on forced arbitration. “I never expected to come before this body to talk about its use against 9-year-olds, but that’s where we are.”

Roblox is currently facing nearly 200 lawsuits from families who allege that their children were groomed by sexual predators posing as children on the platform. According to Hawley, Roblox CEO David Baszucki was invited to testify at the hearing but declined.

“He may think he’s silent, but in fact he’s testifying, and what he’s testifying to is his commitment to money over people,” Hawley said.

In a statement, Sara Kanawati Stephany, a senior manager for US policy communications at Roblox, told WIRED, “Safety has been central to Roblox since we launched. We require age checks for chat, place users under 16 in age-based accounts with protective defaults, and block images and video in chat. A legal position about arbitration is not a measure of a company’s safety record, and a hearing built around it fails to advance safety. Protecting children online takes stronger protections, better tools, and consistent standards that apply everywhere kids spend time online.”

Roblox has previously argued that users waive their right to sue in open court in the platform’s terms of agreement. According to Roblox’s own data, 35 percent of its age-checked daily active users are under the age of 13—too young to fully comprehend the terms of the agreement, witnesses argued.

“There is no way an 8-year-old could read those terms and then sign away their right to a moment in court, effectively silencing themselves,” Republican senator Katie Britt said after being presented with a copy of the multi-page agreement.

Two of those who testified before Congress were alleged survivors of grooming on the platform. One was Michael Schlep, a content creator who has advocated for more stringent child safety measures on the platform.

Schlep testified that when he was 12, he met a game developer on the platform who befriended him in a public chatroom, then moved to private chats. He alleges he was exposed to “violent pornography, cartel beheadings, and extreme racist ideologies” that he says was a result of his communication with this adult man, and that his abuser exposed his private information, leading to a suicide attempt. He currently runs a YouTube channel exposing alleged Roblox child predators and criticizing the platform for failing to protect children, which has led to Roblox hitting him with a cease-and-desist.

“Roblox must be held accountable publicly,” Schlep testified. “They will not voluntarily act to protect children.”

The hearing also featured testimony from a Marine Corps veteran identified as Woody Doe, who alleged that he was groomed, then sexually assaulted by an adult man he met on Roblox when he was 11 years old. “For years, I carried the shame of what happened,” he testified. He now has a lawsuit pending against Roblox for allegedly failing to warn parents and children of the dangers of the platform.

“I cannot go back and protect the 11-year-old boy I once was, but I can speak for him today … and prevent any other children from ever experiencing the same pain,” he said.

Roblox is a massive gaming platform, with about 138 million daily active users according to recent company data. As of 2025, 39.7 million daily active users were under the age of 13.

In response to the litigation and to intense media scrutiny, Roblox has adopted what it says are more stringent child-safety measures, including AI-assisted face recognition to estimate a user’s age. But Khari James, senior legal counsel at the National Center on Sexual Exploitation said face-recognition technology isn’t always accurate, and predators could potentially purchase verified accounts to continue to prey on children. Doing face verifications just once, she argues, gives predators “complete access to all the children on Roblox.”

“Roblox may be a virtual world, but the children are real,” James said during her testimony. “The predators are real. The addiction is real. The exploitation is real, and the consequences are real. Children should never have to enter a game marketed to them and wonder whether the person on the other side of the screen is there to play with them or prey on them.”

#346. Ways to tell if someone blocked your phone number on iPhone

A missing read receipt or an unanswered FaceTime call could mean a block, or it could just be a bad signal.

Let's be very clear about this — if someone has blocked your phone number, whether on iPhone or Android, that's their right and you shouldn't disregard it. They probably don't want to talk to you, and deliberately trying to circumvent that could constitute harassment, maybe even at the criminal level. It's better to just move on.

That said, there's no inherent harm in trying to determine if you've been blocked. It may even be crucial if you have an honest reason to think it was a mistake. While blocking a number by accident is unlikely, it's not impossible.

Since you're using an iPhone, the clues are mostly in Apple's Phone, Messages, and FaceTime apps. But you may want to expand your sleuthing to third-party messaging platforms, depending on how you previously communicated with someone.

Your biggest clue is likely to be a call in the Phone app that goes straight to voicemail after one ring or no ring at all. You can only be sure after multiple calls at varying hours, however. That's because with a single call, or several calls within a short timeframe, there may be alternative explanations. Perhaps the person has Do Not Disturb or another Focus mode on. It could also be that their cellular or Wi-Fi signal is bad, that their phone is off or even that they're in the middle of an iOS or Android update, which requires a lengthy reboot.

A faster way of confirming things is by calling from a second number if you have one, such as Google Voice or a work phone. Exercise caution here, since this could be seen as harassment. Passive options are always preferable. Besides, if someone knows (or knew) you well enough, there's a good chance they've blocked all your normal contact options.

Further signs that you've been blocked could include FaceTime calls failing to connect, or absent read receipts in the Messages app even though it's been hours or days since your last text. Once again, there may be other issues at play. Apart from bad signal quality or a phone being turned off, if they're an iPhone owner, it could be that they've disabled iMessage, or that Apple's servers are temporarily offline. Android phones won't provide receipts at all unless they're using RCS instead of SMS.

While third-party apps like WhatsApp, Signal and Telegram are often linked to your phone number, blocking someone via iOS settings doesn't affect those apps, for the simple reason that they rely on frameworks beyond Apple's control. Missing read receipts or unanswered calls could be evidence that you've been blocked across multiple platforms. However, they might mean something else, such as Meta or Telegram experiencing technical difficulties.

You also can't read too much into automated replies, regardless of the app. They can, however, be used as a kind of "soft" block, discouraging you from calling or texting without seeming so harsh. If you're encountering an iPhone's automatic call screening when it wasn't there before, the other person may have deleted you from their Contacts app, which could make it the most obvious sign that you should stop.

#343. Hundreds of websites deliver potent malware cocktail to unsuspecting visitors

Malware cocktail delivers cryptocurrency theft payloads and iOS exploits, among other things.

Optimizely serves JavaScript “snippets” that include both company code and code that is provided by each customer. The JavaScript, which can be served directly from Optimizely or from a customer endpoint, runs on every page the customer serves. Somehow, the attackers wrote their own code into a portion of each affected customer’s JavaScript and then delivered it from cdn.optimizely.com. A valid certificate for that domain signed the JavaScript.

ReportURI researcher Scott Helme said the delivery mechanism wasn’t a CDN cache poisoning attack, which uses HTTP to cause a CDN to cache harmful responses. Instead, the attack relied on Optimizely’s legitimate infrastructure, including its domains, to serve the tainted code. Optimizely’s own customer JavaScript for the www.optimizely.com and login.optimizely.com URLs were also affected.

“We don’t know how the attacker got write access to so many unrelated customer projects: a compromised Optimizely system, a compromised credential with cross-customer access, or something else,” ReportURI Helme wrote. “That’s for Optimizely to explain.”

Optimizely representatives didn’t respond to questions sent by email.

The scripts were named track.js, and all four components became active at the same time. Devices that received the malicious code responded differently depending on their platform and what they were doing on the final page delivering it. Actions performed included:

1. Crypto wallet address swapping. The script searches for wallet addresses for nine different cryptocurrencies and, when found, replaces them with one of the attacker’s. ReportURI said funds have already been stolen from some people whose devices ran the code.

2. Card skimming. The script watches HTTP requests for payment card numbers, expiry dates, and CVVs. When all three are present, it sends them to https://1688360.cc/card.php. Cards entered in hosted payment iframes such as Stripe and Adyen were unaffected.

4. The DarkSword and Coruna exploit kits for iOS. The kits are delivered through a file named boot.js served from 5vobauua3ojpklx.icu and eil786npto9u5bq.icu. The file delivers a hidden iframe that contains an exploit chain tailored to the iOS version being used. Coruna can infect iOS versions 13 to 17. DarkSword can infect versions 18.x. A separate chain for iOS 26 fingerprints devices but doesn’t appear to do anything else. Earlier this month, researchers saw hackers possibly linked to the Kremlin attempting to deliver DarkSword through multiple vectors, including a compromised web analytics service.

The list of sites that ReportURI found delivering the malicious scripts numbers 178, and as noted, includes many big names. It’s unclear if the list is exhaustive. Helme said in an interview that “Ars wasn’t affected as far as we saw, and I haven’t seen any other indications it was.” Website administrators can check both the ReportURI post and this one from security firm Cynet for indicators of compromise.

At the moment, there’s no information available on how successful the exploit chains were in installing the payloads. Beyond the bare-bones details above, more precise information about what versions of iOS were susceptible was also unavailable. These sorts of gaps are common in breaking news concerning mass malware attacks, because it takes time for researchers to sift through the evidence. Readers are encouraged to check back as new developments come to light.

The indicators may help end users determine if they are affected, but the skill required is likely out of reach for many.

#342. Intelligent women get less help at work, study finds

Women who scored high on intelligence tests were seen as more hostile by their teammates and got less help, a new study finds. High-scoring men faced no such penalty. Research explains why.
